title: Saffron rice (chelow)
subtitle: Persian steamed rice with golden crust
excerpt: The foundation of Persian cooking: basmati rice parboiled, drained, then steamed slowly with saffron butter until the bottom forms a golden, crispy crust called tahdig. The rice is fluffy above, crackling and golden below.
sourceNotes: Chelow is the foundational rice preparation of Persian cuisine. Described in detail in Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (2011), and in classical Persian culinary traditions dating to the 19th century.

glossaryTerms.definition: The golden, crispy rice crust that forms at the bottom of the pot when Persian chelow is made. Considered the most prized part of the dish; it is served by inverting the pot onto a platter or scooped out separately.
Plain steamed Persian rice, typically prepared with a tahdig (crispy crust), served as the base for Iranian dishes with stew (khoresh) or kebabs alongside.

content.text: is Persian steamed rice: parboiled, drained, and then steamed over low heat for 30 to 40 minutes until the grains are long, fluffy, and separate, and the bottom layer has formed a golden crust called
. Saffron butter poured over the top colours part of the rice a deep gold.

The tahdig is the coveted part. It comes away from the pot in a single sheet if you have got the temperature and timing right. Getting it right takes one or two attempts; the method is not difficult once you know what to look for.

items.prepNote: rinsed until the water runs clear, then soaked 30 minutes if time allows
steeped in 3 tbsp hot water for 10 minutes

content.text: Bring a large saucepan of water to a rolling boil. Add the salt. Drain the soaked rice and add it. Boil for exactly 5 minutes. The grains should be barely tender on the outside with a firm white core inside.
Drain through a colander and rinse briefly with cold water. The rice should feel firm.
Return the saucepan to medium-high heat. Add the oil and 20 g butter. When the butter has melted and the pan is hot, spoon in the rice, building it into a loose pyramid. Work quickly.
Use the handle of a spoon to poke 4 or 5 holes down through the rice to let steam escape. Melt the remaining 40 g butter and mix with the saffron water. Pour half over the rice.

Wrap the lid in a clean tea towel and place it firmly on the pan. This absorbs the steam and prevents condensation dripping back onto the rice. Cook on medium-high for 3 minutes until you hear sizzling, then reduce to the lowest possible heat. Steam for 30 to 35 minutes.
Remove the pan from heat and rest for 5 minutes. Pour the remaining saffron butter over the fluffy rice in the pan.

To serve, spoon the fluffy rice onto a platter first. Then run a thin spatula around the sides of the pot and invert the golden tahdig crust onto the platter alongside the rice, or break it into pieces and scatter over the top.

items.symptom: No tahdig formed; the bottom is pale and soft
items.cause: Heat was too low from the start, or not enough oil
items.fix: Increase the initial heat. The sizzle in the first 3 minutes is essential to start the crust forming.

items.symptom: The tahdig is burnt and bitter
items.cause: Heat was too high or it steamed too long
items.fix: The crust should be golden, not brown. Reduce heat and check at 25 minutes next time.

items.symptom: The rice grains are clumping and gluey
items.cause: Parboiled too long or rice was not rinsed well
items.fix: Rinse rice thoroughly until the water runs clear. Parboil for no more than 5 minutes.

items.symptom: The tahdig stuck to the pot and broke apart
items.cause: Normal with a stainless pan; non-stick pans release more cleanly
items.fix: Use a non-stick pan or run cold water over the outside of the pan for 30 seconds after removing from heat; the thermal shock helps release the crust.

content.text: Chelow is the rice every Iranian home cook makes. It sits alongside khoresh (stew) or kebabs, and the tahdig is shared among guests, often given to the most honoured person first. Most rice traditions use simple absorption; chelow uses a two-stage technique that produces a texture unlike anything else.
